questions.text: According to “The Intelligence Gap”, what does a computer actually understand?
options: Concepts like distance and speed, as long as the hardware is fast enough
Plain natural language, given enough processing power
An Instruction List (IL) — extremely fundamental operations executed at blistering speeds
High-level Python code, which it runs directly on the CPU
questions.explanation: Slide “The Intelligence Gap”: computers lack innate intelligence and do not understand distance or speed. They only understand an Instruction List (IL) of extremely fundamental operations, and humans must provide the IL.

questions.text: Computers have innate intelligence, so they can work out what to do without anyone giving them an Instruction List.
questions.explanation: Slide “The Intelligence Gap”: computers lack innate intelligence — humans must provide the IL. Without a program, even the most powerful computer is just a space heater.

questions.text: In the slide's analogy, a computer without a program is like…
options: A piano without a player — just a wooden box
A player without a piano — all skill, nothing to play on
questions.explanation: Slide “The Intelligence Gap”: “Without a player, a piano is just a wooden box. Without a program, the most powerful computer is just a space heater.” The piano is the hardware (object); the sheet music is the program (instruction list).

questions.text: Match each layer of the funnel in “Distilling Thought into Execution” to its description.
allChoices: The bridge — uses symbols and human-readable conventions (source code)
The CPU's mother tongue — rudimentary (machine code)

pairs.match: The bridge — uses symbols and human-readable conventions (source code)
The CPU's mother tongue — rudimentary (machine code)

questions.explanation: Slide “Distilling Thought into Execution”: natural language at the top, a high-level language like Python as the bridge in the middle, and machine language — the CPU's mother tongue — at the bottom.

questions.text: Why do we need a high-level programming language at all?
options: Because machines already understand natural language, but too slowly
Because we can't speak directly to machines and they can't learn our natural languages, so we need a bridge
Because machine code is too fast for the CPU to keep up with
Because high-level languages skip translation and run on the hardware directly
questions.explanation: Slide “Distilling Thought into Execution”: we cannot speak directly to machines, nor can they learn our natural languages. A high-level language acts as a bridge, distilling abstract human goals into concrete machine instructions.

questions.text: Human-readable code written in a high-level language like Python is called ___ code.
questions.explanation: Slide “Distilling Thought into Execution”: the high-level language layer is labelled “Source Code”; the bottom layer is machine code.

questions.text: According to “The Translation Matrix”, which of these describe an interpreter like Python? (Select all that apply.)
options: Stops immediately at the broken line
Faster, because the code is pre-translated
Requires a full compilation before errors are found
questions.explanation: Slide “The Translation Matrix”: the interpreter translates line-by-line in real time, is slower (translating on the fly), stops immediately at the broken line and is highly portable. Pre-translated speed, hardware-specific output and full compilation before errors are found are the compiler's column.

questions.text: Which is the compiler's advantage over an interpreter in “The Translation Matrix”?
options: It is highly portable across platforms
It stops immediately at the broken line
It executes faster, because the code is already pre-translated
It translates line-by-line as the program runs
questions.explanation: Slide “The Translation Matrix”: a compiler translates all at once, so execution is faster (pre-translated). The interpreter is slower because it translates on the fly.

questions.text: A compiler's output is highly portable across platforms, while an interpreter is hardware-specific.
questions.explanation: It's the other way round. Slide “The Translation Matrix”: compiler — hardware-specific; interpreter (Python) — highly portable across platforms.

questions.text: What is an IDE, as described in the slides?
options: An Integrated Development Environment — your digital workbench for writing source files
An Interpreted Data Engine that turns Python into machine code ahead of time
An Instruction Definition Editor used only for machine code
An Internal Debugging Extension built into the CPU
questions.explanation: Slide “The Translation Matrix”: “You write source files in an IDE (Integrated Development Environment — your digital workbench), and Python translates them line-by-line as the program runs.”

questions.text: What does the interpreter do with line 2 of this program?
questions.context:
# Coffee Shop ASCII Logo
# This is a comment. The interpreter ignores it.

print('  (  )  (  )')
print('   ) (   ) (')
print(' ..........')
print(' |        |]')

print('Welcome to Bean Cafe!')
options: Prints it to the console before the logo
Ignores it — comments are for humans, code is for machines
Raises a SyntaxError because it isn't inside print()
Saves it as the program's title
questions.explanation: Slide “Speaking to the Console”: a line starting with # is a comment, and the interpreter ignores it. “Comments are for humans. Code is for machines.”

questions.text: Fill in the character that turns this line into a comment.
questions.code:
___ Coffee Shop ASCII Logo
print('Welcome to Bean Cafe!')
questions.explanation: Slide “Speaking to the Console”: in Python, everything after a # on a line is a comment.

questions.text: In “Speaking to the Console” (Scenario 2: System Boot-up Greeting), what is the program's goal?
options: Ask the barista for their name and store it in a variable
Print a textual ASCII logo when the POS terminal turns on, so the barista knows the system is ready
Calculate the day's sales total and print a receipt
Shut the POS terminal down safely at closing time
questions.explanation: Slide “Speaking to the Console”: “Goal: Print a textual ASCII logo when the POS terminal turns on so the barista knows the system is ready.” It's done entirely with print() calls.

questions.text: Match each value from “The Memory Box Model” to its kind of literal.
questions.explanation: Slide “The Memory Box Model”: 25 is an integer literal, 5.9 a float literal and 'Alex' a string literal.

questions.text: In age = 25, what are age and 25?
options: age is a literal; 25 is a variable
age is a variable (the container); 25 is a literal (the raw data put in it)
questions.explanation: Slide “The Memory Box Model”: to remember anything, we tell the computer to create a specific container (a variable) and fill it with a specific type of raw data (a literal).

questions.text: The user types 50 at the prompt. What does this program print?
questions.context:
# Tax Calculator

base_price = float(input('Enter base price: '))
tax_rate = 0.08

total = base_price + (base_price * tax_rate)
print('Total Due: $', total)
questions.explanation: Slide “Computation and Ingestion”: 50 + (50 × 0.08) = 54.0 — a float, because base_price was converted with float(). print() puts a space between its comma-separated arguments, hence $ 54.0. Verified by running it.

questions.text: What does input() do?
options: Prints a value to the console
Pauses the program to ingest data from the human
Converts text into a decimal number
Reads the next line from a file on disk
questions.explanation: Slide “Computation and Ingestion”: “input() pauses the program to ingest data from the human.” What it hands back is always a string, which is why the tax calculator wraps it in float() before doing arithmetic.

questions.text: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Slide “Computation and Ingestion”: // is floor division, which drops the remainder (17 // 5 = 3), and % is modulo, which keeps only the remainder (17 % 5 = 2). Verified by running it.

questions.text: Match each arithmetic operator to what it does.
questions.explanation: Slide “Computation and Ingestion”, Python Arithmetic Operators panel: + add, - subtract, * multiply, / divide, // floor division (drops remainder), % modulo (keeps only the remainder).

questions.text: What does this print?
questions.context:
score = 85

if score >= 90:
    print('Grade: A')
elif score >= 80:
    print('Grade: B')
elif score >= 70:
    print('Grade: C')
else:
    print('Grade: F')
questions.explanation: Slide “Routing Logic with Conditionals”: score >= 90 is False, score >= 80 is True, so Grade: B prints. Even though score >= 70 is also true, Python takes only the first True branch and ignores the rest entirely. Verified by running it.

questions.text: Relational operators like >= evaluate to boolean values (True or False), which Python uses to decide which block of code to run.
questions.explanation: Slide “Routing Logic with Conditionals”: relational operators evaluate to booleans, and Python uses them like switches on a train track, deciding which block to execute and which to ignore.

questions.text: Match each description from “The Loop Decision Engine” to the loop it describes.

pairs.term: Sequence-based — iterates through a known range
Condition-based — loops as long as a boolean is True

questions.explanation: Slide “The Loop Decision Engine”: for is sequence-based with a fixed count; while is condition-based with an indefinite count.

questions.text: A program has to keep reading a sensor until the temperature drops below 30°C — nobody knows how many readings that will take. Which loop fits?
options: A for loop, because it is sequence-based
A while loop, because you're waiting for a condition to change
questions.explanation: Slide “The Loop Decision Engine” takeaway: use for when you know exactly how many items to process; use while when you are waiting for a specific condition to change.

questions.text: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Slide “The Loop Decision Engine”: range(3) produces 0, 1 and 2. It starts at zero and stops before 3. Verified by running it.

questions.text: What does this print?
questions.explanation: The while example from “The Loop Decision Engine”, with count = 0 added so it runs. It loops while count < 3: 0→1, 1→2, 2→3, then 3 < 3 is False and the loop ends, so 3 prints. Verified by running it.

questions.text: What does manifest[1:3] give you?
questions.explanation: Slide “The Indexing Train (Lists)”: the slice starts at index 1 (part_240) and stops before index 3, so it takes indexes 1 and 2. Verified by running it.

questions.text: Fill in the reverse index that reaches the last car of the train, however long the list is.
questions.explanation: Slide “The Indexing Train (Lists)”: part_999 sits at Index [3] / Reverse Index [-1]. Negative indexes count back from the end, so -1 is always the last item.

questions.text: Python lists start counting at one, so manifest[1] is the first item.
questions.explanation: Slide “The Indexing Train (Lists)”: “Lists are dynamic arrays. They always start counting at zero.” manifest[0] is the first item.

questions.text: What does 'part_240' in manifest do in this code?
questions.context:
manifest = ['part_101', 'part_240', 'part_330', 'part_999']
if 'part_240' in manifest:
    print('Part is in today\'s delivery.')
options: Checks whether 'part_240' is one of the list's items, giving True or False
questions.explanation: Slide “The Indexing Train (Lists)”: in tests membership and evaluates to a boolean. Here it's True, so Part is in today's delivery. prints. Verified by running it.

questions.explanation: Slide “The Data Structure Selector”, Syntax Definition row.

questions.text: Match each use case to the data structure “The Data Structure Selector” recommends for it.

pairs.term: Looking up an employee ID to find their department

questions.explanation: Slide “The Data Structure Selector”, Ideal Use Case row: lists for changing items, tuples for fixed data that should never change, dictionaries for key lookups.

questions.text: Which of these data structures are mutable (can be changed after they're created)? (Select all that apply.)
questions.explanation: Slide “The Data Structure Selector”, Mutability row: lists — yes (dynamic); tuples — no (immutable); dictionaries — yes (dynamic). Trying t[0] = 1 on a tuple raises TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment (verified by running it).

questions.text: How are values in a dictionary accessed?
options: By numerical index, starting at zero
Only by looping over every value in order
By their position counted from the end
questions.explanation: Slide “The Data Structure Selector”, Access Method row: lists and tuples are accessed by numerical index; dictionaries by key lookup.

questions.text: What does this print?
questions.context:
multiplier = 5

def multiply_number(num):
    return num * multiplier

print(multiply_number(10))
questions.explanation: Slide “Functions and The Walled Garden”: code inside a function can see out and use global variables, so 10 × 5 = 50. Verified by running it.

questions.text: After calling the function, the main program tries print(num). What happens?
questions.context:
multiplier = 5

def multiply_number(num):
    return num * multiplier

multiply_number(10)
print(num)
options: It raises NameError, because num is local to the function
questions.explanation: Slide “Functions and The Walled Garden”: variables created inside a function (local) belong only to that walled garden. The function can see out, but the global program can't see in, so print(num) raises NameError: name 'num' is not defined. Verified by running it.

questions.text: What do safe_divide(10, 4) and safe_divide(10, 0) return?
questions.context:
def safe_divide(a, b):
    try:
        return a / b
    except ZeroDivisionError:
        return 'Error: Cannot divide by zero!'
options: 'Error: Cannot divide by zero!' both times
questions.explanation: Slide “The Broken Rail (Exception Handling)”: 10 / 4 = 2.5 (/ always gives a float). Dividing by zero raises ZeroDivisionError, which the try-except block catches and reroutes to the safe track instead of crashing. Verified by running it.

questions.text: Match each part of the program in “Anatomy of a Robust Program” to the role it plays.
questions.context:
employees = {'1001': 'Eng', '1002': 'Sales'}

def lookup_employee(emp_id):
    try:
        dept = employees[emp_id]
        print('Employee in', dept)
    except KeyError:
        print('ID not found.')

search_id = input('Enter ID: ')
lookup_employee(search_id)
questions.explanation: Slide “Anatomy of a Robust Program” labels each block: the dictionary stores the state, the function modularizes the action, try/except protects the flow and input() bridges to the human.

questions.text: Using the same program, the user types 1003. What is printed?
questions.context:
employees = {'1001': 'Eng', '1002': 'Sales'}

def lookup_employee(emp_id):
    try:
        dept = employees[emp_id]
        print('Employee in', dept)
    except KeyError:
        print('ID not found.')

search_id = input('Enter ID: ')
lookup_employee(search_id)
questions.explanation: Slide “Anatomy of a Robust Program”: '1003' isn't a key, so employees[emp_id] raises KeyError, which the except block catches. Typing 1001 would print Employee in Eng — the keys are strings, which matches what input() returns. Verified by running it.

questions.text: According to “From Object to Engine”, what turns a lifeless machine into an intelligent engine?
options: Memorising a long list of Python vocabulary words
Combining variables, loops, conditional logic and robust exception handling
Switching from an interpreter to a compiler
questions.explanation: Slide “From Object to Engine”: you haven't just learned vocabulary — you've learned to build a complete sentence. Combining variables, loops, conditional logic and robust exception handling gives you the tools to transform a lifeless machine into an intelligent engine.
